examples.knowledge_point: Projecting a Vector Onto a Perpendicular Vector
examples.problem: Let ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14046465/assets/e477b14c9148f4132c747a358e1e99f76d40df85b82c66d6e7dd38581b33913c.png) and ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14046465/assets/b17d86e3e395b2fd752f5529090c0a5e4e2fdce17642be5594bee98e8c47fed2.png) Find the scalar projection of $\mathbf{a}$ onto $\mathbf{b}.$
examples.worked_solution:
Using the formula for the scalar projection, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{b}\,a & =\frac{a\cdot b}{|\,b\,|} \\  & =\frac{{a}_{x}{b}_{x}+{a}_{y}{b}_{y}+{c}_{z}{b}_{z}}{\sqrt{{b}_{x}^{2}+{b}_{y}^{2}+{b}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{0\cdot 2+0\cdot (-4)+1\cdot 0}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-4)^{2}+{0}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{0}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+(-4)^{2}+{0}^{2}}} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
Using the formula for the scalar projection, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{q}\,p & =\frac{p\cdot q}{|\,q\,|} \\  & =\frac{{p}_{x}{q}_{x}+{p}_{y}{q}_{y}+{p}_{z}{q}_{z}}{\sqrt{{q}_{x}^{2}+{q}_{y}^{2}+{q}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1\cdot (-7)+\sqrt{6}\cdot \sqrt{6}+3\cdot 3}{\sqrt{(-7)^{2}+{\sqrt{6}}^{2}+{3}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{8}{\sqrt{64}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

and

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{p}\,q & =\frac{p\cdot q}{|\,p\,|} \\  & =\frac{{p}_{x}{q}_{x}+{p}_{y}{q}_{y}+{p}_{z}{q}_{z}}{\sqrt{{p}_{x}^{2}+{p}_{y}^{2}+{p}_{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{8}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{\sqrt{6}}^{2}+{3}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{8}{\sqrt{16}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{comp}}_{q}\,p+{\text{comp}}_{p}\,q & =1+2 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$
